Face Recognition Using Graph Neural Networks in PyTorch¶

Abstract¶

This Project shows you how to build and train a graph neural network (GNN) in PyTorch to perform face validation using MediaPipe face landmark graphs. When given a picture of a random face, the model can correctly classify whether the face is mine or not. The pipeline for this tutorial includes loading data from our custom dataset and training and validation functions, which are called in our epoch loop. We show in graphs and a confusion matrix the learning curve and class prediction. This demonstrates that the model is learning.

Learning Objectives¶

After completing this tutorial, you will have an understanding of:

  • How to build a machine learning pipeline in PyTorch
  • Train a graph neural network for binary classification
  • Understand how hyperparameters affect training performance
  • Visualise model results using graphs and other evaluation metrics

Introduction¶

Facial Recognition is an important task in computer vision and has many application such as surveillance. Traditional approaches rely on Convolutional neural networks (CNN) that learn features from 2D images. We will explore an alternative approach using a Graph Neural Network. Instead of relying purely on pixel information, we extract 3D landmark features using Google’s Meidapipe face mesh.

These 3D features will be represented in a graph, where each face landmark becomes a node, and the connections between these nodes form edges. This allows the model to learn structural relationships among facial features, such as the nose, eyes, and mouth. which can be far stronger for real-time validation. So in this tutorial, you will learn how to use data to train a Neural Network in PyTorch.

Google’s Mediapipe¶

We extract facial landmarks using Google’s Mediapipe faceMesh framework. The faceMesh creates a mesh of the face it has been given, and detects 468 landmarks on that face. These landmarks correspond to key facial features that the model uses to learn patterns to differentiate between faces, such as the jawline, mouth, nose, eyes, etc, and then returns each landmark’s spatial coordinates. Each landmark on the face is used as a node in our graph. The predefined connections between landmarks will be used as our edges in our graph.

Google’s Mediapipe is well documented at [https://ai.google.dev/edge/mediapipe/solutions/vision/face_landmarker/python]. And you can test it on their website here [https://mediapipe-studio.webapps.google.com/demo/face_landmarker].

To keep focused on the machine learning pipeline, the graphs have been pre-generated and stored as .pt files in the folder /face-features. These .pt files consist of 3D coordinates for each landmark, e.g. x and y being the landmark's position and z being the depth.

This code below demonstrates how MediaPipe detects facial landmarks from an image and draws the FaceMesh. I have shown two images to show how it works across different faces and head positions.

In [1]:
# Example adapted from the MediaPipe Face Landmarker documentation:
# https://ai.google.dev/edge/mediapipe/solutions/vision/face_landmarker
# The code has been simplified and modified to visualise FaceMesh landmarks
# on multiple images for this tutorial.
import cv2
import mediapipe as mp
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Initialise MediaPipes FaceMesh model
mp_face = mp.solutions.face_mesh
face_mesh = mp_face.FaceMesh(static_image_mode=True, max_num_faces=1)
image = ["image.jpg","image2.jpg"]
plt.figure(figsize=(10,5))  
for i, img in enumerate(image):
    face = cv2.imread(img)
    rgb = cv2.cvtColor(face, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)
    results = face_mesh.process(rgb)
    if results.multi_face_landmarks:
        for face_landmarks in results.multi_face_landmarks:
            mp.solutions.drawing_utils.draw_landmarks(
                image=face,
                landmark_list=face_landmarks,
                connections=mp_face.FACEMESH_TESSELATION,
                landmark_drawing_spec=mp.solutions.drawing_utils.DrawingSpec(
                    color=(255, 0, 0), thickness=1, circle_radius=1
                ),
                connection_drawing_spec=mp.solutions.drawing_utils.DrawingSpec(
                    color=(70, 50, 255), thickness=1
                )
            )
            

    # showing results side by side 
    plt.subplot(1, 2, i+1)
    plt.imshow(cv2.cvtColor(face, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB))
    plt.axis("off")
plt.figure(figsize=(5,5))
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Dataset¶

In this folder, I have given a dataset.py, which loads all of the graph features from the face_feature folder. The graphs are already separated into two classes: class 0, my face and class 1, not my face.

The "not me" class was constructed from Celeba dataset available on Kaggle. This dataset contains a large number of celebrity images of their face. This was important because it provided the model with diverse negative samples, which improves the model's ability to correctly distinguish "my face" from other faces.

When the dataset reads the graph files, it also reads the parent folder, which allows it to create labels for each graph and returns it into a format that can be used in training.

The dataset also splits the graph features into training, validation and test sets, using a 70/15/15 split. Data loaders are created for each split so that the graphs can be loaded in batches during training and validation.

First, we need to load the graph features into this notebook

if torch.cuda.is_available():
    device = "cuda"
elif torch.backends.mps.is_available():

else:
    device = "cpu"
print(f"Using {device} device")

Using cpu device

Graph Neural Network Model¶

For the model given, it has 3 graph layers and two fully connected layers at the end. In between each layer, we will use the ReLU function because having multiple GNN layers is mathematically the same as having one layer, so the ReLU function acts as a break that prevents this. I have also used GraphNorm; it normalises features within each graph. This can help training become more stable.

The first and second layers are graph convolutional networks (GCN). It processes data by allowing each node to learn directly from its neighbours. The reason we stack the GCN is so that the network can capture information from increasingly wider neighbourhoods. The third layer I used is a graph attention network convolutional. This layer expands on the GCN layer by adding attention mechanisms to the message passing process. It improves upon the GCN layers by allowing nodes to dynamically learn which neighbours are most important for learning about them. While the GCN layer treats all neighbours with a fixed degree of importance.

At the end of the forward function, the model has global mean pooling, which calculates the average of all node features in the graph, and max pooling, which takes the maximum for each feature. And concatenating them at the end means we can use both instead of having to choose. This pooling is to create a single representation of the face graph.

The fully connected layers at the end of init convert the pooled graph representations into class predictions.

In [7]:
@torch.compile # this compiles the code into optimised execution graphs, so PyTorch can run the model more efficiently 
class GNN(torch.nn.Module):
        def __init__(self):
            super(GNN, self).__init__()
            # First GCN layer with GraphNorm
            self.conv1 = SAGEConv(3, 128, aggr="mean")
            self.bn1 = GraphNorm(128)
           
            # Second GCN layer with GraphNorm
            self.conv2 = SAGEConv(128, 64, aggr="mean")
            self.bn2 = GraphNorm(64)
            
            # GAT layer with GraphNorm
            self.conv3 = GATConv(64, 128, heads=1, concat=True)
            self.bn3 = GraphNorm(128)

            # fully connected layers 
            self.fc1 = torch.nn.Linear(128, 64)
            self.fc2 = torch.nn.Linear(64, 2)


        def forward(self, data):
            x, edge_index = data.x, data.edge_index

            # First GCN layer with ReLU and GraphNorm
            x = F.relu(self.conv1(x, edge_index))
            x = self.bn1(x)
            x = F.dropout(x, p=0.2, training=self.training)

            # Second GCN layer with ReLU and GraphNorm
            x = F.relu(self.conv2(x, edge_index))
            x = self.bn2(x)
            x = F.dropout(x, p=0.2, training=self.training)

            # GAT layer with GraphNorm
            x = F.elu(self.conv3(x, edge_index))  # ELU can be used for a change
            x = self.bn3(x)
            x = F.dropout(x, p=0.2, training=self.training)

            # Global mean pooling
            x = global_mean_pool(x, data.batch)
            # x_max  = global_max_pool(x, data.batch)
            # x = torch.cat([x_mean, x_max], dim=1)

            # Fully connected layers
            x = F.relu(self.fc1(x))
            x = self.fc2(x)

            return x


model = GNN().to(device)
#model = torch.compile(model)
print(model)

GNN(

  (conv2): SAGEConv(128, 64, aggr=mean)
  (bn2): GraphNorm(64)
  (conv3): GATConv(64, 128, heads=1)
  (bn3): GraphNorm(128)
  (fc1): Linear(in_features=128, out_features=64, bias=True)
  (fc2): Linear(in_features=64, out_features=2, bias=True)

Optimising Weights and Biases¶

For training this model, we need a loss function to keep track of learning progress and an optimiser to update the model's parameters.

The loss function we are using here is CrossEntropyLoss. It compares the model's prediction with the correct class label and calculates how far the model is from the correct answer. The model then updates its weights accordingly to minimise this loss during training. A small weight has been put on class 0. Class 0 is the face class we are trying to recognise, so we want the model to predict class 1 when unsure.

The optimiser used it, AdamW, which adjusts the learning rate during training. Weight decay helps regulate the model by preventing the weights from becoming too large.

In [8]:
loss_fn = torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss(weight=torch.tensor([1.1, 1.0]).to(device))
optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=0.0005, weight_decay=0.001)

Training Function¶

This function, defined below, will be used in our epoch iteration to pass the data through the model so it can learn from the training data. This is where the model predicts which class each feature belongs to for the training data. It uses backpropagation to propagate the prediction error back to the optimiser so it can adjust its weights.

In [9]:
def train_model():
        model.train() # setting the model to training 
        total_loss = 0.0
        total_graphs = 0

        for data in train_loader:
            data = data.to(device)
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            logits = model(data)  # forward pass through the GNN defined above 
            loss = loss_fn(logits, data.y)
            loss.backward() # backpropagation to update weights 
            torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0) # stabilise training by limiting gradient size
            optimizer.step()
        
            # track loss for all graphs in the batch 
            total_loss += loss.item() * data.num_graphs
            total_graphs += data.num_graphs
            
        # returning the average training loss 
        return total_loss / max(1, total_graphs)

Evaluation Function¶

We need to make sure the model works properly. We define an evaluation function which checks the model’s performance against the validation data. It does not update the model’s weights and does not perform backpropagation.

We split the data into batches, like in the training function. The model produces predictions which are then compared against the true labels to compute the loss and performance metrics. The predictions are then converted into probabilities using a SoftMax function.

We also compute and return other accuracy metrics, which are precision, recall, and F1 score. so they can be used to monitor the model’s learning on the training and validation set.

In [10]:
@torch.no_grad() # no_grad disables gradient calculations during evaluation to reduce memory usage. 
def eval_metrics(loader, model, device):
    model.eval() # setting the model to evaluation mode 
    # Defining evaluation metrics 
    total_loss = 0.0
    total_examples = 0
    all_preds = []
    all_labels = []
    all_probs = []

    

    for data in loader:
        data = data.to(device)
        logits = model(data) # forward pass through the model               
        loss = loss_fn(logits, data.y)
        bs = data.y.size(0)
        total_loss += loss.item() * bs     
        total_examples += bs

        # turning our forward pass into probabilities and predicted classes
        probs = torch.softmax(logits, dim=1)
        preds = probs.argmax(dim=1)
        all_preds.append(preds.cpu())
        all_labels.append(data.y.cpu())
        all_probs.append(probs[:, 1].cpu())

    # combining all batches into a single numpy array    
    all_preds = torch.cat(all_preds).numpy()
    all_labels = torch.cat(all_labels).numpy()
    all_probs = torch.cat(all_probs).numpy()
    # prints models prediction distribution to monitor if the model is biased or if it collapses to predicting one class
    print("Pred counts:", Counter(all_preds))
    print("True counts:", Counter(all_labels))

    # calculating loss and accuracy
    avg_loss = total_loss / max(total_examples, 1)
    acc = (all_preds == all_labels).mean()

    # calculating macro F1 score for evaluation 
    # zero_division avoids warnings when a class gets no predictions early on
    precision_macro = precision_score(all_labels, all_preds, average="macro", zero_division=0)
    recall_macro    = recall_score(all_labels, all_preds, average="macro", zero_division=0)
    f1_macro        = f1_score(all_labels, all_preds, average="macro", zero_division=0)



    return avg_loss, acc, precision_macro, recall_macro, f1_macro, all_preds, all_labels, all_probs

Create History List For Results, Defining Early Stopping, and Saving The Model¶

We define some lists to store training and validation history so we can plot them in graphs later.

In [11]:
# storing history for graph vars 
train_loss_history = []
val_loss_history = []
train_acc_history = []
val_acc_history = []
train_f1_history = []
val_f1_history = []
lr_history = []

# saving model variables
best_overall = -1.0
best_ckpt = None
best_seed = None
# early stopping variables to stop the model from overfitting  
patience = 3
min_delta = 1e-3
best_val_f1 = -1.0
best_state = None
epochs_without_improvement = 0

Epoch iterations¶

We train the model for many epochs. In each epoch, the model updates its parameters by repeatedly passing over the data, which in turn improves predictions.

At each epoch, we will print the model’s training and validation loss and accuracy, along with their F1 scores. We want to see the loss decrease while the accuracy increases. We can calculate a baseline for loss and accuracy to analyse early results.

Because this is a binary classification problem, we want the validation and training loss to start below ln(2) = 0.69314718056. And we would like to see the accuracy above 1/2 = 0.5 = 50% for the first couple of epochs, the 50% accuracy is considered random learning. This means that if the accuracy is 50%, then it’s performing at a chance level.

We also append the training and validation data to the lists we defined earlier so we can plot learning curves later.

In [12]:
# start of the epoch loop for 50 epochs 
for epoch in range(1, 51):
    start = time.time()
    train_loss = train_model()  # calling the training function, which trains the model on the training data

    # This is where we call the evaluation function on the training and validation data, so we can compare them later and track performance 
    train_loss_eval, train_acc, train_precm, train_recm, train_f1m, _, _, _ = eval_metrics(train_loader, model, device)
    val_loss, val_acc, val_precm, val_recm, val_f1m, y_pred, y_true, y_probs = eval_metrics(val_loader, model, device)

    # here we append the history to our lists we made earlier
    train_loss_history.append(train_loss)
    val_loss_history.append(val_loss)

    train_acc_history.append(train_acc)
    val_acc_history.append(val_acc)

    train_f1_history.append(train_f1m)
    val_f1_history.append(val_f1m)

    
    #This is how we track the best model to save. 
    #We check if the validation F1 score for that run is greater than the current best F1 score minus 1e-3 (0.001). 
    if val_f1m > best_val_f1 - min_delta: 
        best_val_f1 = val_f1m
        epochs_without_improvement = 0
        best_state = {k: v.detach().cpu().clone() for k, v in model.state_dict().items()}
    # If this criterion is not met, we increment the epochs_without_improvement variable by 1.
    else:
        epochs_without_improvement += 1

    # This is where we check whether we have gone too many epochs without improvement, then we stop. Our patience is set to 3
    if epochs_without_improvement >= patience:
        print(f"Early stopping at epoch {epoch} (no improvement for {patience} epochs)")
        break

    epoch_time = time.time() - start # calculating run time per epoch
    # displaying training and validation metrics. 
    print(f"Ep {epoch:03d} | TrainLoss {train_loss:.4f} | ValLoss {val_loss:.4f} | "
          f"TrainAcc {train_acc:.3f} | ValAcc {val_acc:.3f} | "
          f"TrainF1(macro) {train_f1m:.3f} ValF1(macro) {val_f1m:.3f} | time {epoch_time:.2f}")

Early stopping at epoch 13 (no improvement for 3 epochs)

The output above shows that the model is learning, as the training and validation losses decrease and accuracy increases. The best validation score is reached at epoch 10, with 85.7% validation accuracy and 85.7% validation F1 score. Early stopping is triggered at epoch 9 after no improvement in validation accuracy for 3 epochs, which helps to prevent overfitting.

Loading The Best Model and Evaluating It on Training Data Set¶

Here, we check and make sure there is a best state for the model; if there is, we then return it. and call the evaluation function to see how it performs on unseen data (test dataset).

In [13]:
# restore best for this seed
if best_state is not None:
    model.load_state_dict(best_state)
else:
    raise RuntimeError("No best model state was saved during training.")

# evaluate best-restored model on test
test_loss, test_acc, test_precm, test_recm, test_f1m, _, _, _ = eval_metrics(test_loader, model, device)
print(f"TEST: loss={test_loss:.4f} acc={test_acc:.3f} f1={test_f1m:.3f} | bestValF1={best_val_f1:.3f}")

Results¶

Training vs Validation Loss¶

The graph below shows how training and validation losses change over epochs. The loss is measured by how far the model prediction is from the true label, so a decrease in loss shows good performance.

At the start, the training and validation losses are high, indicating that the model is learning from the data. As the training goes on, the training loss and validation loss should decrease, which shows the model is improving its predictions.

If the training and validation loss curve is similar shows the model is learning generalizable features rather than just memorising the training data.

If the training loss decreases and the validation loss increases, this suggests the model is overfitting. This is where it memorises the training data and does not learning it.

In [14]:
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
plt.plot(train_loss_history, label="Training Loss", color='blue')
plt.plot(val_loss_history, label="Validation Loss", color='red',
         linestyle='dashed')
plt.xlabel("Epochs")
plt.ylabel("Loss")
plt.title("Training vs Validation Loss")
plt.legend()
plt.grid()
plt.show()

Training vs Validation Macro F1¶

This graph shows the macro F1 score for both the training and validation datasets across the training history. The F1 score is calculated by multiplying precision and recall and then dividing by the sum of them. Macro F1 then provides a balanced measure of the model's accuracy.

As epochs increase, so does both F1 scores’ increase, showing the model is learning how to correctly classify the classes {0,1}. If the validation F1 scores’ curve follows a similar trend to the training, then the model is learning useful patterns from the training data.

In [15]:

plt.plot(val_f1_history, label="Validation Macro F1", linestyle="dashed")

plt.ylabel("Macro F1")
plt.title("Training vs Validation Macro F1")
plt.legend()

Confusion Matrix¶

Below is a confusion matrix, which measures the model's predicted label count compared to the true label count. It helps show how well the model performs and whether it is biased towards one class. In this confusion matrix, the rows are the true labels and the columns are the model's predicted labels.

The top left quadrant shows how many samples the model correctly classified as "not me". The bottom left quadrant shows False Negatives, which is how many times the model predicted "not me" when the true label was "me".

The bottom Right box shows how many samples were correctly classified as "me". The top right box shows the opposite, which are false positives. This is where the model predicted me when the image was actually "not me"

This also allows us to calculate precision and recall. Precision TP \ TP + FP and recall = TP \ TP + FN

from the confusion matrix, if the \ diagonal numbers are large and the boxes are darker, then this shows that many samples were classified correctly. This would show that the model is performing well and is able to distinguish between the two classes. If the / diagonal has the larger numbers and darker colour, then this would show the model is making many mistakes and cannot correctly predict between the two classes. This should not be the case.

In [16]:
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, ConfusionMatrixDisplay

cm = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred)

disp = ConfusionMatrixDisplay(confusion_matrix=cm, display_labels=["Not Me", "Me"])
disp.plot(cmap="Blues")
plt.title("Confusion Matrix")
plt.show()

True vs Predicted Class Distribution¶

This is a simple bar chart which helps us visualise the balance between the true count and the predicted count. The orange bars show the model's predicted sample count, and the blue bars show the true sample count. We want to see the orange "me" bar lower than the blue, because we do not want a model to falsely predict it is "me" when it is "not me". then for the "not me" bars, we would see the opposite.

The predicted counts are close to the true counts, which means the model is not overall biased towards one class and the predictions roughly match the true class distribution.

pred_vals = [pred_counts[0], pred_counts[1]]

width = 0.35

plt.bar(x + width/2, pred_vals, width, label="Predicted Count")

Hyperparameter Comparison (Class Weights)¶

Model Configuration Precision (Me) Recall (Me) False Positives False Negatives F1 Score
No Weights 0.86 0.87 13 12 0.87
With Weights 0.88 0.83 11 16 0.85

The table above shows the effect of adding class weights to the loss function. The weighted model reduces false positives from 13 to 11, meaning it is less likely to incorrectly predict "me" for a different person. This is very important for facial recognition so we don't misclassify people.

This improvement is also reflected in the precision, which increased from 86% to 88%, showing that predictions of "me" are more reliable. However, this comes at a cost of recall, which drecreased form 87% to 83%. meaning the model misses more true "me"'s. Increasing the class weights shifts the model towards higher precision at the expense of recall. resulting in the model only predicting me when confidence is high.

In the context of face validation systems. Reducing false positives is more important than maximising recall, this is because identifying another person as "me" is worse than missing a correct match. To conclude, the weighted model is more appropriate for this face validation system, and this highlights how even small changes in hyperparameters can influence the model's behaviour.

The images above show the trained model applied and working in a real-time scenario. The model correctly identifies my face on the left with high confidence, while correctly classifying an unseen face as "unknown".

This shows the model learns meaningful patterns and facial features rather than just memorising the training set. The ability to reject an unknown face is important because it reduces false positives and increases the system's reliability. Overall, these results support the quantitative evaluation metrics above.

Differences From Existing Tutorials with Pros and Cons¶

This Tutorial builds on ideas from existing tutorials such as PyTorch Geometric GNN tutorials and MediaPipe guides. I will explain some key differences.

Compared tutorial source: PyTorch Quickstart Tutorial (https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/basics/quickstart_tutorial.html)

  1. Use of Graph Neural Networks: Most tutorials use convolutional neural networks on raw images, but we use graph neural networks.

Advantage:

  • Using GNNs gives us a more meaningful representation, i.e. only the key facial structure instead of the full raw image.
  • We can capture the relationships through edges.

Disadvantages:

  • GNNs are more complex than a traditional CNN-based approach.
  • It also requires custom data preprocessing.
  1. Use of Google's MediaPipe FaceMesh: instead of training directly on image pixels. This tutorial uses MediaPipe to extract 468 facial landmarks and build graphs from them.

Advantages:

  • This reduces the input size, which increases training speed.
  • Focuses on only facial features rather than full images.

Disadvantages:

  • Rely on external preprocessing
  • Errors in landmark detection can affect the model's performance.
